entries.title: Monterey Canyon
paragraphs: Monterey Canyon begins just offshore of Moss Landing, beside the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI). Its walls reach about 1,700 m from floor to rim. MBARI describes a main channel extending more than 470 km offshore, continuing through the Monterey Deep Sea Fan and ending below 4,000 m on the abyssal plain.

Sediment supplied from nearby beaches accumulates at the canyon head. Storm waves and slope failures can turn it into turbidity currents: fast underwater flows of sediment and seawater. Earthquakes can trigger sediment flows, but none of the flows in the 2015–2017 Coordinated Canyon Experiment coincided with earthquakes above magnitude 2, and some powerful flows occurred without major external triggers. These flows continue to carve and reshape the canyon.
This tile covers the upper canyon to about 2,333 m depth. The deeper channel and its continuation across the deep-sea fan lie beyond the western edge of the survey.

Secret finds and wildlife encounters in this dive are plausible game additions rather than documented sightings at their displayed positions. The species tables preserve an OBIS snapshot from 23 September 2026: counts measure sampling effort, and depths are sampled occurrence ranges rather than full habitat limits. The shared comb-jelly label is uncertain here: northeastern Pacific Bolinopsis are B. microptera, distinct from the Atlantic B. infundibulum.

entries.title: The canyon head
paragraphs: Monterey Canyon's head lies right off the beach at Moss Landing. The seafloor here drops away steeply, and MBARI's research vessels can reach areas more than a mile deep in a little over two and a half hours.
This closeness to shore helps explain why the canyon is so well studied: deep-sea habitats and processes are within easy reach of MBARI's shore-based marine laboratory.

The scan point samples the upper canyon's GMRT terrain at about 44 m depth. Its previously reported distance of about 2.5 km offshore is an unverified estimate, rather than a measured position of the canyon's shoreline head.

facts.value: about 2.5 km previously estimated; unverified shoreline reference

entries.title: A canyon wall
paragraphs: From the axis out to the rim, Monterey Canyon's walls climb as much as about 1,700 m, comparable to the depth of the Grand Canyon. Along the way they are cut by smaller side gullies, and repeated small slope failures feed sediment into the turbidity currents that scour the canyon floor below.

This point samples the canyon's north wall at about 748 m depth. An earlier terrain trace estimated a nearby axis roughly 700 m away and 270 m lower; those cross-section estimates remain unverified because the comparison axis point is no longer retained in this pack.

entries.title: Following the canyon floor
paragraphs: The canyon's axis, or thalweg, is its deepest, most continuously carved line -- the path a turbidity current follows on its way downhill. Tracing it through this tile's survey data shows a fairly steady deepening from the shallow head out past 2,000 m, punctuated by side channels and terraces where sediment has piled up between major flow events.

In the Coordinated Canyon Experiment, researchers deployed moorings and seabed instruments along a 50 km stretch of Monterey Canyon. They measured turbidity-current fronts moving at up to about 7.2 m/s (16 mph). Some flows travelled at least 50 km down-canyon.
These sediment flows also carry organic carbon from coastal waters to the deep sea, supplying food to organisms far below the sunlit surface.

facts.value: up to about 7.2 m/s (Paull et al. 2018)

entries.title: The upper canyon descent
paragraphs: A few kilometres down-canyon from the head marker, this tile shows the bottom dropping from about 44 m to 265 m over about 2.85 km in a straight line. The descent exposes the steep channel within the continental shelf; depth alone does not establish the regional shelf-break position.

An earlier description identified this scan point as the shelf break. That identification remains unverified. The upper channel carries sediment toward deeper water and is close enough to the head marker for a short dive before continuing toward the deeper wall and the MARS observatory farther offshore.
This point is real GMRT terrain, traced by sampling depth along the line from the canyon head toward the axis.

entries.title: MARS: a deep-sea power outlet
paragraphs: The Monterey Accelerated Research System (MARS) is a cabled seafloor observatory: a science node on the continental slope in Monterey Bay connected to shore by a 52 km (32 mi) power and data cable. It converts 10,000 volts from shore down to 375 and 48 volts DC for scientific instruments, and offers up to 100 megabits per second of data bandwidth per instrument across eight ports, so researchers can run experiments for months or years without worrying about battery life.

Its trawl-resistant frame, about 3.7 by 4.6 m at the base and 1.2 m tall, has smoothed corners and sloping sides so fishing gear and anchors slide off rather than snag, while still letting a remotely operated vehicle open its side doors to plug in new instruments.

MARS went live on 10 November 2008, following NSF support for its development from 2002. It sits at 891 m depth, about 34 km in a straight line from this mission’s canyon-head marker. Its shore cable follows a longer, curved route to avoid rocky ground and landslide hazards.
